On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated in a television interview that the administration wants answers from Nvidia regarding chip sales to China: who was monitoring compliance with the rules and which levels of the company knew.

The affair is weighing on the markets. On Friday, Nvidia stock lost around 13% following news that the SEC, the US stock market regulator, is examining the company's accounting, according to two sources cited by the press. The slump in artificial intelligence-related stocks swept across Wall Street and Asian stock markets, where among the causes cited by analysts is precisely the scandal involving Nvidia, which has reopened calls for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced chips.

According to the Departments of Commerce and Justice, the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over possible export control violations. Alice Huang was questioned during an on-site inspection in June 2025; the criminal case was subsequently referred to the Department of Justice. An associate of Huang, Li Ming, is out on bail in Singapore: the city-state's charges relate to alleged false declarations to Super Micro Computer and do not name Megaspeed. Singapore police said they found insufficient evidence of offences linked to inaccurate statements by Huang, who received a stern warning for providing information believed to be knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role. Singapore has not investigated her for espionage.

According to a US press report, Alice Huang was allegedly in contact with an official from a major Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 to autumn 2026; there is no official confirmation. According to another account, the Department of Justice is verifying whether companies linked to Huang helped ship Super Micro products out of the US to China. The president of COP31 in Antalya, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, wants to bring the third draft of the final decision to the plenary without further changes. According to European delegation sources, the European Union intends to vote against, and under the consensus rule this is enough to prevent approval. Kurum says there is a broad consensus, with a few minor open issues, and that those blocking the process should reflect on their position.

The draft, presented overnight between Saturday and Sunday, does not explicitly mention the phase-out of fossil fuels, but recalls «in its entirety» the UAE Consensus, the final document of COP28 in Dubai in 2023. That text provided for the transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems by 2050. Kurum says he is convinced the text is acceptable to all parties.

Negotiations, involving almost 200 delegations, were scheduled to end on Friday 20 November and have continued for a second day past the deadline. Delegations could submit objections until 3 am Greenwich Mean Time on Sunday, and the session to begin approval was set for 6 am, 7 am in Italy. Decisions are taken by consensus: an objection from a single country can block them.

The French Minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, called the proposal a step backwards and said «time is running out and we are not there yet». Thursday's draft had removed all references to fossil fuels following objections from Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers, drawing strong criticism. One hundred civil society organisations wrote to Turkey and Australia, who are leading the negotiations, warning that the summit risks being «one of the most disappointing COPs» ever organized by the UN. The European Union is calling for an explicit commitment to phase out fossil fuels; the Arab group of countries and Russia refuse to include it.

The third draft, in Article 38, calls for the «full and rapid» implementation of nationally determined contributions, namely each country's climate commitments, and of national adaptation plans. Kurum states that the text also addresses the concerns of developing countries regarding adaptation funding. According to reports, discussions remain open on how much effort to ask from countries to reduce coal, oil and gas, whether to encourage carbon capture and storage, and whether the expansion of electricity should be based solely on renewables or also on gas and coal.

This is the first COP since the UN confirmed that global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree limit of the Paris Agreement.

The UN climate summit, COP31, closed on Sunday 22 November in Antalya, Turkey, without a final agreement, after a prolonged extension. The text presented by the co-presidencies of Turkey and Australia was rejected by the European Union and other countries because it made no mention of fossil fuels. According to sources' reconstructions, it is the first failure of an annual climate conference since the Copenhagen summit in 2009.

The draft would have recognised for the first time in an official text that global warming is on a trajectory exceeding 1.5 degrees. In the revised version, the target of 120 billion dollars to help poor countries adapt had been removed. Delegates from various countries described the text as too weak to address warming.

The European Union said it would not approve an agreement «that does not even mention fossil fuels». Denmark's Climate Minister, Samira Nawa, explained that the EU would have accepted the clauses on adaptation funds, but that strong commitments on emission reductions and reference to science were lacking. For British negotiator Kate Hughes, the draft «takes us backwards from the science».

The front opposed to the word «fossils» includes oil- and gas-producing countries. The Saudi Arabian delegation said that «climate change requires all solutions on the table» and that «concrete solutions» must not be taken away. The Russian delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, said Russia «cannot accept any wording on fossil fuels», warning that less oil and gas supply could lead to energy poverty. Iraq expressed «deep concern» over passages it said move away from the Paris Agreement.

Island and most vulnerable nations spoke of betrayal. The Marshall Islands say they were «disappointed by all sides», Vanuatu called the silence on fossils unacceptable, and the group of least developed countries, 44 nations with over a billion inhabitants, said it could not accept steps backwards. Kenya complained that the text did not respond to Africa's needs.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was «deeply disappointed». Chris Bowen, Australia's Climate Minister and chair of the negotiations, said that «an obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels» and that some parties would veto any text mentioning it. Murat Kurum, the Turkish Environment Minister and president of COP31, said there will be no new text and that work will focus on implementing decisions already taken.
